title: Commentariorum In Epistolam Beati Pauli Ad Galatas Libri Tres
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp483.tmp483.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Vanos Mauros, et feroces Dalmatas, Latinus pulsat histo- ricus. Timidos Phrygas, omnes poetae lacerant. Athenis expeditiora nasci ingenia, philosophi glo- riantur. Graecos leves, apud C. Caesarem sugillat Tullius, dicens : Aut levium Graecorum, aut immanium barbarorum. Et pro Flacco : Ingenita, inquit, levitas, et erudita vanitas. Ipsum Israel, gravi corde, et dura cervice, omnes Scripturae arguunt. In hunc ergo mo- dum arbitror et Apostolum 417 Galatas regionis suae proprietate pulsasse.
passages.english: The Latin historian strikes at the Moors as vain and the Dalmatians as fierce. All the poets tear at the Phrygians as timid. The philosophers boast that readier talents are born at Athens. Tully, speaking before Gaius Caesar, taunts the Greeks as fickle, saying: "Either of the fickle Greeks or of the savage barbarians." And in the speech for Flaccus he says: "Inborn fickleness and learned vanity." All the Scriptures reproach Israel itself for a heavy heart and a stiff neck. In the same way, then, I think the Apostle too struck at the Galatians for the peculiar character of their region.
passages.notes: "417" is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: Sed quia nobis propositum est, incircumcisos homines non introducere in tem- plum Dei (et ut simpliciter fatear, multi jam anni sunt quod haec legere desivimus), Lactantii nostri quae in tertio ad Probum volumine dc hac gente opi- natus sit, verba ponemus : c Galli, inquit, antiquitus a candore corporis Galatae nuncupabantur; et Sibylla sic eos appellat. Quod significare voluit poeta, cum ait Tumlactea colla—Auro innectuntur (Virg. lib. viii AEneid.) : Cum posset dicere, candida. Hinc utique Galatia provincia, in quam Galli aliquando ve- nientes, cum Graecis se miscuerunt.
passages.english: But since it is our purpose not to bring uncircumcised men into the temple of God (and, to confess it plainly, it is many years now since I stopped reading these things), we will set down the words of our Lactantius, giving what he thought about this people in the third volume addressed to Probus: "The Gauls," he says, "were in ancient times called Galatae from the whiteness of their bodies, and the Sibyl calls them so. This is what the poet meant to indicate when he says, 'then their milk-white necks are bound with gold' (Virgil, Aeneid book 8), when he could have said 'white.' From this, certainly, [comes the name of] the province of Galatia, into which the Gauls came at one time and mingled with the Greeks.
passages.notes: The stray "c" before "Galli" is a printed footnote mark and is omitted; "dc" read as "de". The Lactantius quotation continues into the following passage. The name derives from Greek gala, "milk".

passages.original: Nec mirum si hoc ille de Galatis dixerit, et Occi- dentales populos tantis in medio terrarum spatiis praetermissis, in Orientis plaga consedisse memo- rarit : cum constet Orientis contra et Graeciae exa- mina, ad Occidentis ultima pervenisse. Massiliam Phocaei condiderunt : quos ait Varro trilingues esse, quod et Graece loquantur, et Latine, et Gallice. Op- pidum Rhoda, coloni Rhodiorum locaverunt : unde a amnis Rhodanus nomen accepit. Praetermitto Car- thaginis conditores Tyrios, et Agenoris urbem;
passages.english: Nor is it surprising if he said this about the Galatians, and recorded that Western peoples, passing over such great stretches of land in between, settled in the region of the East, since it is well established that, conversely, swarms from the East and from Greece reached the farthest parts of the West. The Phocaeans founded Massilia; Varro says they are trilingual, because they speak Greek, Latin and Gaulish. Colonists of the Rhodians established the town of Rhoda, from which the river Rhodanus took its name. I pass over the Tyrians, founders of Carthage, and the city of Agenor;
passages.notes: The stray 'a' before 'amnis' is a footnote mark and has been omitted. Massilia is Marseille; Rhoda is Rhode (modern Roses); the Rhodanus is the Rhône. 'He' is the source Jerome quotes in the preceding context (the Varro-like authority on the name Galatae).

passages.original: 4.) At ubi venit plenitudo temporis, misit Deus Filium suum factum ex muliere, facium sub Lege : ut eos qui sub Lege erant, redimeret, ut adoptio- nem filiorum reciperemus. Diligenter attendite quod non dixerit, factum per mulierem : quod Marcion et caeterae haereses volunt, quae putativam Christi carnem simulant; sed ex muliere, ut non per il· lam, 449 sed ex illa natus esse credatur. Quod autem sanctam et bea'am Matrem Domini, mulie- rem, non Virginem nominavit, hoc idem et in Evan- gelio χατά Ματθαίον scriptum est : quando uxor ap- pellatur Joseph (Luc, ii), et ab ipso Domino quasi mulier increpatur (Joan.
passages.english: (Verse 4.) But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, so that he might redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons. Pay careful attention to the fact that he did not say 'made through a woman', as Marcion and the other heresies would have it, which feign that Christ's flesh was only apparent; but 'from a woman', so that he may be believed to have been born not through her but from her. As for his calling the holy and blessed Mother of the Lord 'woman' and not 'Virgin', the same is also written in the Gospel according to Matthew, when she is called the wife of Joseph (Luke 2), and when she is rebuked, as a woman, by the Lord himself (John
passages.notes: 'facium' read as 'factum'. Jerome says 'the Gospel according to Matthew' (in Greek), but the edition's marginal reference gives Luke 2; the reference to Joseph's wife fits Matthew 1. The 449 is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted. The sentence breaks off at 'John', and the reference is completed in the following text (2).

passages.original: Quod aulem profecerim ex linguae illius infatigabili studio, aliorum judicio de- relinquo : ego quid in mea amiserim, scio. Accedit ad hoc, quia propter oculorum et totius corpusculi infirmitatem, manu mea ipse non scribo : nec labore et diligentia compensare queo eloquii tarditatem : quod de Virgilio quoque tradunt, quia libros suos in modum ursorum fetum [Al. fetuum] lambendo figu- raverit : verum accito notario, aut statim dicto quod- cumque in buccam venerit : aut si paululum voluero cogitare, melius aliquid prolaturus, tunc me tacitus ille reprehendit, manum contrahit, frontem rugat, et se frustra adesse, toto gestu corporis contestatur.
passages.english: But what I have gained from tireless study of that language I leave to the judgement of others; what I have lost in my own, I know. Add to this that, because of the weakness of my eyes and of my whole poor body, I do not write with my own hand; nor can I make up for slowness of expression by labour and care, as they also report of Virgil, that he shaped his books by licking them, in the way bears [lick] their cubs. Instead, having summoned a secretary, I either dictate at once whatever comes into my mouth, or, if I want to think a little in order to bring out something better, then he silently reproaches me, draws back his hand, wrinkles his brow, and by every gesture of his body declares that he is there for nothing.
passages.notes: "aulem" read as "autem". The edition records a variant "fetuum" for "fetum" (offspring); the sense is the same.

passages.original: Scripsit et beatus Cyprianus librum de Zelo et Li- vare valde optimum; quem qui legerit, non dubi- tabit annumerare operibus carnis invidiam. Inter invidum autem et invidiosum hoc interest : quod invidus feliciori a invidet.
passages.english: The blessed Cyprian also wrote a very excellent book On Jealousy and Envy; whoever reads it will not hesitate to count envy among the works of the flesh. Between the envious man and the envied man there is this difference: the envious man envies one who is more fortunate.
passages.notes: "Livare" read as "Livore". The stray "a" after "feliciori" is a printed footnote mark and is omitted.

passages.original: Unum ver- bum apud Graecos χινόδοξοι, trium verborum cir- cuitu interpres Latinus expressit. Quantas autem habeat definitiones, et significantias gloria, et phi- losophorum innumerabiles libri, el Ciceronis duo volumina, quae de gloria scripsit, inditio sunt. Verum nos quia non verborum etymologias, sed Scripturae sensum disserere conamur, ita hunc lo- cum cum superioribus copulabimus : Si a spiritu vivimus, spiritui obtemperemus, nequaquam per Legem, sed per charitatem nobis invicem servientes.
passages.english: The Latin translator expressed one word in Greek, kenodoxoi, by a circumlocution of three words. How many definitions and meanings 'glory' has is shown by the countless books of the philosophers and by the two volumes Cicero wrote On Glory. But since we are trying to discuss not the etymologies of words but the sense of Scripture, we will join this passage to what precedes it as follows: if we live by the spirit, let us obey the spirit, serving one another not through the Law but through love.
passages.notes: The Greek as printed, "χινόδοξοι", is a scanning error for κενόδοξοι ("vainglorious"); the Latin's three words are "inanis gloriae cupidi" ("desirous of empty glory"). "el" read as "et", "inditio" as "indicio".
